papers.title: Mortality dynamics of West Nile virus and Lyme disease in the United States: Temporal, spatial, and socioeconomic dimensions (2003-2021).
papers.abstract: West Nile virus (WNV) and Lyme disease pose a growing public health threat in the United States. This study investigated spatial and temporal mortality trends of WNV and Lyme disease and evaluated associations with individual and county-level factors. We utilized National Center for Health Statistics data to identify WNV- and Lyme-related deaths (2003-2021), including demographics and the decedent's county of residence. County-level insurance status was sourced from the U.S. Census Bureau, and urbanicity was defined using the 2013 National Center For Health Statistics classification. We applied negative binomial regression models to identify predictors of mortality. Our analysis of 3694 deaths (WNV: 2,628 [71.2%]; Lyme: 1,066 [28.8%]) revealed WNV peaks occurred in 2003 (246 deaths, 9.4% of WNV deaths) and 2012 (281 deaths, 10.7%), and an increasing trend for Lyme (103 deaths, 9.7% in 2021). Overall, deaths were highest in 2012 (343, 9.3%) and lowest in 2009 (105, 2.6%). Age ≥65 (rate ratio [RR] = 1.5, confidence interval [CI] = 1.27, 1.48), male sex (RR = 1.2, CI = 1.04, 1.26), and White race (RR = 1.7, CI = 1.37, 1.73) were associated with increased mortality. Spatial analysis indicated high WNV mortality in California, Colorado, Arizona, and Texas, and states along the Mississippi River. In contrast, Lyme disease deaths were concentrated in the Northeast and the Upper Midwest. Our results suggest that age, sex, race, and urbanicity are important factors influencing mortality from WNV and Lyme disease. More research is needed to link exposures and incidence to mortality of WNV and Lyme to better understand the drivers of regional variation, given the spatial and temporal variability.

papers.title: Not always cancer-Probable Lyme disease mimicking squamous cell carcinoma: A case report.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, can produce head and neck manifestations in up to 75% of cases, most commonly facial palsy and lymphadenopathy. Borrelial lymphoid proliferations are recognized mimics of malignancy; however, tonsillar involvement simulating a malignant neoplasm has not been previously described. We report a 57-year-old male patient who presented with a right cervical lump associated with odynophagia, weight loss, and low-grade fever. PET-CT demonstrated intense FDG uptake in a right palatine tonsillar mass and right cervical lymph nodes, with loss of fat plane definition relative to the adjacent sternocleidomastoid muscle. Subsequent MRI revealed an irregular tonsillar mass with restricted diffusion and heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement of the cervical lymph node conglomerate, with internal areas of necrosis, imaging features highly suspicious for oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with extranodal extension. Histopathological examination of the cervical lymph nodes revealed reactive lymphadenitis, and serological testing detected IgM for Borrelia burgdorferi. The patient was treated with doxycycline and demonstrated significant reduction of the tonsillar mass and cervical lymph nodes at three-month follow-up imaging. This case illustrates that infectious etiologies, even rare ones, can produce imaging findings that closely mimic carcinoma, and reinforces the importance of clinical correlation and imaging follow-up before committing to aggressive treatment.

papers.title: Lyme Disease and Other Tick-Borne Infections.
papers.abstract: The neurologic manifestations of selected tick-transmitted infections in North America and Eurasia were reviewed. Both Powassan virus in North America, and Tick-Borne Encephalitis (TBE) virus in Eurasia can cause encephalitis, often with significant neurologic morbidity. Lyme disease, Ehrlichia chaffeensis (the cause of human monocytic ehrlichiosis [HME]), and Borrelia miyamotoi infections can cause meningitis (the third primarily in immunocompromised individuals). Patients with Lyme disease may also develop cranial neuropathy, and/or radiculoneuropathy. Tick-borne infections are being increasingly recognized in North America and Eurasia. While many tick-borne infections can cause headaches, lethargy or other non-specific symptoms, these are generally not evidence of nervous system infection - i.e., neuroinvasive disease. The latter is less common but may occur in infections due to Powassan and TBE viruses, in HME and in Lyme disease. Patients with symptomatic nervous system infection due to Powassan or TBE virus are at high risk of developing significant neurologic impairment and sequelae.

papers.title: A promoter G-quadruplex recruits Hrb27C to regulate NEMO and immune defense against Lyme disease pathogens in the deer tick.
papers.abstract: Genomic DNA can adopt noncanonical secondary structures, such as G-quadruplexes (G4s), which serve as critical regulatory elements beyond the traditional double helix. Whether promoter G4s also participate in controlling innate immune signaling and host-pathogen interactions, however, remains unknown in arthropods. In this study, we identify a G4 structure within the promoter of the NEMO (NF-κB essential modulator) gene in the deer tick Ixodes scapularis. Using a combination of circular dichroism, isothermal difference spectra, and fluorescence-based assays, we demonstrate that this sequence forms a stable, parallel G4 topology in vitro and in vivo. Functional characterization via luciferase reporter assays reveals that this G4 scaffold is essential for proper NEMO transcriptional output. Importantly, disruption of the G4 structure significantly reduces NEMO expression and increases the burden of the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. Genome-wide expression profiling further reveals that perturbation of the NEMO G4 produces transcriptional changes that overlap with those observed following NEMO silencing. These shared transcriptional responses are enriched for immune-associated genes and ribonucleoprotein-related pathways. We further identify the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein Hrb27C as a structural binding protein that specifically recognizes the NEMO G4 through its RNA recognition motif domains and facilitates NEMO expression. Collectively, our findings establish promoter G4 architecture as an important regulatory layer in tick immunity, linking DNA topology to pathogen proliferation and providing a structural framework for understanding host-pathogen dynamics in disease vectors.

papers.title: Anaplasma spp., Coxiella, Babesia and Theileria Infections in Vermipsylla Alakurt Fleas.
papers.abstract: Vermipsylla alakurt (Siphonaptera: Vermipsyllidae) is mainly distributed in alpine areas of north-western China, infesting sheep, goat and yaks, causing pruritus, anaemia and losses to animal husbandry. The carriage of vector-borne pathogens by this flea remains unclear. In January 2025, 89 fleas were collected from sheep in the China-Kazakhstan border area of northwest China and identified as V. alakurt by morphology and COII gene sequencing. Multiple genetic markers targeting the genera of Anaplasma, Coxiella, Babesia and Theileria were amplified and sequenced. Among 83 female fleas, Anaplasma ovis (n = 6), Coxiella burnetii (n = 37), Babesia sp. (n = 7), Babesia ovis (n = 1) and Theileria annulata (n = 4) were identified. The co-infection of Coxiella burnetii with Anaplasma ovis and Theileria annulata were respectively found. Multiple typical vector-borne pathogens were detected at the first time in V. alakurt fleas. This finding indicates that V. alakurt fleas can carry Anaplasma, Coxiella, Babesia and Theileria in the alpine region of the China-Kazakhstan border.

papers.title: Functional Metagenomics Reveals Gut Microbial Biosynthetic Potential for Essential Nutrients in Juvenile Chum Salmon.
papers.abstract: The fish gut microbiota contributes to host nutrition, immunity and homeostasis, yet how its metabolic capacity relates to gaps in the host genome remains poorly characterized. Here we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing and KEGG module completion analysis to compare the biosynthetic potential of the gut microbiome with that of the host genome in juvenile chum salmon (Oncorhynchus keta) at 35 days posthatching, when exogenous feeding begins. Because small juvenile guts yield low microbial biomass and a high proportion of host DNA, we first optimized a protocol combining enzymatic lysis with NEBNext-based host DNA depletion. This raised the bacterial sequence fraction from 11.3% to 41.2% and increased the number of KEGG Orthology identifiers mapped to modules from 1128 to 1532. Module Completion Ratio analysis revealed complementation in functional potential: the chum salmon genome was incomplete for de novo biosynthesis of essential amino acids (threonine, leucine, valine/isoleucine, lysine) and B-vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin, biotin), whereas the gut metagenome encoded complete or near-complete modules for these pathways. Sequences assigned to Bartonella-like, Acinetobacter and Enterococcus lineages contributed most. These observations indicate that the gut microbiome encodes biosynthetic potential the host genome lacks, although demonstrating a nutritional benefit to the host will require experimental manipulation.

papers.title: Molecular evidence of Bartonella spp. in wild felids from Brazil.
papers.abstract: Among Felidae, domestic cats play a role as reservoirs for Bartonella henselae, Bartonella clarridgeiae, and Bartonella koehlerae. Despite the well-known relationship between Bartonella spp. and domestic cats, to date, there is still a paucity of reports on Bartonella spp. in wild felids. The aim of this study was to molecularly detect and characterize Bartonella spp. in blood and tissue samples from wild felids sampled in Brazil. Among 291 DNA samples (211 blood, 77 spleens and three livers), 3.09% (9/291) were positive in the Quantitative Real-Time PCR (qPCR) assay for Bartonella spp. based on the nuoG gene: 1/44 Leopardus pardalis, 3/61 Leopardus geoffroyi, 1/66 Panthera onca, 1/3 Herpailurus yagouaroundi, and 3/32 Leopardus wiedii. In the phylogenetic analyses, while the gltA sequence detected in L. wiedii grouped with Bartonella henselae, the gltA and ftsZ sequences detected in L. geoffroyi clustered within the same subclade as Bartonella sp. sequences previously identified in wild rodents and associated fleas. These findings reinforce that besides harboring Bartonella species associated with cats, wild felids also may act as accidental hosts for Bartonella species associated with wild small mammals, possibly as a consequence of predation.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Peromyscus leucopus (P. leucopus) is an important reservoir host for several zoonoses, including Borrelia burgdorferi (B. burgdorferi), the causative agent of Lyme disease. However, the immunoglobulin germline repertoire underlying antibody responses in this reservoir host remains poorly defined. In this study, we characterized the immunoglobulin variable genes of P. leucopus and identified 12 IGHV, 12 IGKV, and 3 IGLV gene families comprising 129, 87, and 12 genes, respectively. These genes exhibited similar usage patterns to those of Mus musculus (M. musculus). We also identified a high-divergence region (HDR) within the germline IGHV loci of three Borrelia sp.-susceptible Cricetidae species, P. leucopus, Peromyscus maniculatus (P. maniculatus), and Arvicola amphibius (A. amphibius). Compared with the corresponding regions in Muridae species, the Cricetidae HDRs are expanded and contain a large number of IGHV genes. To investigate the antigen-specific features of the repertoire, we analyzed the antibody responses of P. leucopus to B. burgdorferi outer surface protein A (OspA), a highly immunogenic tick midgut adhesin involved in midgut colonization. Comparative analysis of more than 140 IGHV genes from immunized P. leucopus showed that germline IGHV genes encoding anti-OspA antibodies exhibited higher sequence similarity to corresponding germline IGHV genes in P. maniculatus and A. amphibius than did P. leucopus germline IGHV genes not associated with anti-OspA responses.IMPORTANCEThis study characterized the immunoglobulin gene repertoire of Peromyscus leucopus and revealed extensive diversity across its variable-region loci. Analysis of antibody response to outer surface protein A (OspA) showed that germline IGHV genes encoding anti-OspA antibodies showed higher sequence similarity to their corresponding germline IGHV genes in other Borrelia-susceptible cricetid rodents, suggesting that conserved germline IGHV features are associated with OspA recognition. These findings lay the foundation for further understanding of antibody responses in this important reservoir host.

papers.title: [Bed bugs, lice and fleas-an up-to-date overview of diagnosis, treatment and prevention].
papers.abstract: Despite high standards of hygiene, ectoparasites remain a significant issue in dermatology. Bedbugs (Cimex lectularius) have become significantly more prevalent worldwide over the past two decades, whilst head lice infestation (Pediculus humanus capitis) remains one of the most common parasitic infections in children. Pubic lice (Pthirus pubis) are predominantly transmitted sexually. Body lice (Pediculus humanus corporis) are rare in Central Europe, but remain of infectious disease significance as vectors of Rickettsia prowazekii, Bartonella quintana and Borrelia recurrentis. Flea bites in humans are now predominantly caused by the cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis). The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic cases through papular and urticarial reactions to bullous arthropod reactions and bacterial superinfections. Diagnosis is based on medical history, clinical findings and the direct detection of parasites, nits or characteristic environmental traces. Dermoscopy facilitates the differentiation of live parasites from nits and pseudonits, particularly in cases of pediculosis. Treatment for lice infestations comprises topical pediculicides and physically acting preparations. In the case of bedbug and flea infestations, consistent environmental control measures are crucial for long-term therapeutic success; in the case of flea infestations, concurrent veterinary treatment of infested pets is also essential. This article summarises the current state of knowledge regarding the epidemiology, biology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment and prevention of these medically important ectoparasitic infestations. Ektoparasiten stellen trotz hoher Hygienestandards weiterhin ein relevantes Thema in der Dermatologie dar. Bettwanzenbefälle (Cimex lectularius) haben in den vergangenen 2 Jahrzehnten weltweit deutlich zugenommen, während der Kopflausbefall (Pediculus humanus capitis) unverändert zu den häufigsten parasitären Erkrankungen im Kindesalter zählt. Filzläuse (Pthirus pubis) werden überwiegend sexuell übertragen. Kleiderläuse (Pediculus humanus corporis) sind in Mitteleuropa selten, besitzen jedoch als Vektoren von Rickettsia prowazekii, Bartonella quintana und Borrelia recurrentis weiterhin infektiologische Bedeutung. Flohstiche beim Menschen werden heute überwiegend durch den Katzenfloh (Ctenocephalides felis) verursacht. Das klinische Spektrum reicht von asymptomatischen Verläufen über papulöse und urtikarielle Reaktionen bis hin zu bullösen Arthropodenreaktionen und bakteriellen Superinfektionen. Die Diagnostik basiert auf Anamnese, klinischem Befund sowie dem direkten Nachweis von Parasiten, Nissen oder charakteristischen Umweltspuren. Die Dermatoskopie erleichtert insbesondere bei Pedikulosen die Differenzierung vitaler Parasiten von Nissen und Pseudonissen. Die Therapie umfasst bei Läuseinfestationen topische Pedikulozide und physikalisch wirkende Präparate. Bei Bettwanzen- und Flohbefall sind konsequente Umgebungsmaßnahmen sowie beim Flohbefall die veterinärmedizinische Mitbehandlung befallener Haustiere entscheidend für den nachhaltigen Therapieerfolg. Der Beitrag fasst den aktuellen Kenntnisstand zu Epidemiologie, Biologie, Klinik, Diagnostik, Therapie und Prävention dieser wichtigen humanmedizinisch relevanten Ektoparasitosen zusammen.

papers.title: Development and Evaluation of an RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a Molecular Assay for Rapid Diagnosis of Theileria annulata Infection in Bovines.
papers.abstract: Tropical theileriosis, caused by Theileria annulata, continues to be the most significant tick-borne disease affecting cattle, particularly in endemic regions where it leads to significant production losses. Prompt and reliable diagnosis is critically important for timely treatment and disease control; however, conventional diagnostic methods have important limitations. Microscopic examination lacks sensitivity, particularly in carrier animals, while PCR requires specialized laboratory infrastructure. To overcome these limitations, a fluorescence-based RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay targeting the multicopy mitochondrial cytb gene was developed for rapid detection of T. annulata. Five RPA primer pairs were designed and evaluated, and primer set-5, generating a 324-bp amplicon, exhibited the best amplification performance. A CRISPR RNA (crRNA) was designed within the selected amplicon to enable specific Cas12a-mediated target recognition. The assay was completed within 50 min and demonstrated no cross-reactivity with DNA from Theileria orientalis, Babesia bigemina, Babesia bovis, Anaplasma marginale, and bovine host DNA, confirming excellent analytical specificity. Sensitivity analysis using recombinant plasmid DNA demonstrated a detection limit of approximately ten copies per reaction. The field evaluation of the assay was done by testing 206 bovine field samples. showed that the developed assay identified 163 positive samples, exceeding the detection rates obtained by PCR (151 positives) and microscopy (116 positives). On comparison with PCR, the assay achieved 100% diagnostic sensitivity, 78.18% specificity, 92.64% positive predictive value, 100% negative predictive value, with an overall agreement of 94.17%. These findings indicate that the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a platform is a rapid, sensitive, and accurate molecular diagnostic approach with strong potential for field application and point-of-care diagnosis of bovine tropical theileriosis, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

papers.title: Laboratory larval exposure to mixed-size polystyrene micro/nanoplastics disrupts lipid metabolism and reshapes the hemolymph metabolome and gut microbiota of adult honeybee workers.
papers.abstract: Micro/nanoplastics are pervasive contaminants in terrestrial ecosystems, yet their developmental toxicity to pollinators remains insufficiently understood. Here, worker larvae of the honeybee (Apis mellifera) were orally exposed under controlled laboratory conditions to a mixed-size polystyrene micro/nanoplastic (PS-MNP) system containing 50 nm, 100 nm, and 5 μm particles at a 1:1:1 mass ratio across 1-500 mg/L. Survival was assessed using 48 larvae per group, and adult hemolymph metabolomics and gut microbiome analyses were conducted for adults derived from the 10 mg/L larval exposure group using six biological replicates per treatment. Larval PS-MNP exposure reduced survival, transiently increased larval body mass, and disrupted nutrient allocation, as reflected by decreased total protein and free fatty acids but increased glycogen and triglyceride. In the larval fat body, PS-MNPs induced oxidative stress and lipid droplet accumulation, accompanied by transcriptional changes consistent with enhanced lipid storage and impaired lipophagy. These developmental disturbances were followed by post-metamorphic effects. Newly emerged workers exhibited midgut injury and oxidative imbalance. Moreover, adults derived from exposed larvae displayed pronounced hemolymph metabolomic reprogramming and altered gut microbiota after colony reintroduction. More than 1200 differential hemolymph metabolites were detected, with downregulated features enriched mainly in lipid-remodeling, eicosanoid-related, and autophagy-associated pathways. The adult gut microbiota showed depletion of Gilliamella apicola and Bartonella apis and enrichment of Lactobacillus apis and Frischella perrara. Collectively, these findings show that larval-only exposure to a mixed-size PS-MNP system can disturb developmental lipid/redox homeostasis and be followed by intestinal, hemolymph metabolic, and gut microbial alterations after metamorphosis. This integrated cross-stage evidence advances understanding of micro/nanoplastic developmental ecotoxicology in beneficial terrestrial insects and provides evidence for considering developmental windows in future pollinator risk assessment.

papers.title: Comprehensive Assessment of Babesia gibsoni Infection in Dogs: Clinicopathological, Imaging, and Oxidative Stress Perspectives.
papers.abstract: The present study investigated clinico-pathological alterations associated with naturally occurring Babesia gibsoni infection in dogs from Mizoram, India. Diagnosis was established using rapid antibody detection, microscopic blood smear examination, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Blood samples were collected to study the haemogram, and serum samples were used for the evaluation of serum biochemical profile and oxidant-antioxidant indices. Abdominal ultrasonography was performed in the infected dogs. Of 138 samples screened, 43 (31.15%), 70 (50.72%), and 85 (61.59%) were positive by rapid antibody test, blood smear examination, and PCR, respectively. The most consistent clinical signs included depression/lethargy, inappetence/anorexia, and pyrexia. Splenomegaly and splenic lesions were the most consistent ultrasonographic findings noticed. Major haemato-biochemical alterations comprised anaemia, leukocytosis with neutrophilia and eosinophilia, thrombocytopaenia, hypoproteinaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia, azotaemia, and increased alanine aminotransferase (ALT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Dogs with B. gibsoni infection exhibited significantly (P < 0.001) higher lipid peroxide (LPO) levels and significantly (P < 0.001) lower total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) and reduced glutathione (GSH). Red blood cell (RBC) count showed a negative correlation with LPO (r = - 0.741; P < 0.01) and a positive correlation with GSH (r = 0.714; P < 0.01) and T-AOC (r = 0.828; P < 0.01), indicating a role of oxidant-antioxidant imbalance in the severity of anaemia. These findings underscore the multiorgan involvement of the disease and suggest a potential role of oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of B. gibsoni-induced anaemia in dogs.

papers.title: In vitro induction of the sexual stage of Babesia ovata enhances infection efficiency of Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks in a semi-artificial feeding model.
papers.abstract: Haemaphysalis longicornis is an important tick species that transmits multiple pathogens to animals and humans, and its global distribution is expanding. Understanding tickpathogen interaction requires efficient tick infection models. However, a cost-effective, rapid, and easy-to-operate model remains lacking. This study aimed to improve the infection efficiency of a semi-artificial feeding model by in vitro induction of Babesia ovata using dithiothreitol. Induction was confirmed by morphological observation, reverse transcription-quantitative PCR analysis of sexual-stage marker genes (HAP2, 6CYS, CCP2, and CCP3), and immunofluorescence detection of HAP2 and CCP3 proteins. Ticks were subsequently fed blood containing induced or non-induced B. ovata (at 1-2% or 4-5% parasitemia) or red blood cell controls. Infection rates were assessed by nested PCR detection of B. ovata in tick embryo samples. Embryos derived from ticks that fed sexually induced parasites exhibited significantly higher infection rates compared to those from ticks that fed non-induced parasites (18.87% (10/53) vs. 1.92% (1/52), p = 0.0080). The highest infection rate (22.22% (6/27)) occurred in the induced 1-2% parasitemia group, with no infection detected in controls. These findings demonstrate that in vitro induction of B. ovata sexual stage enhances tick infection efficiency. Incorporating sexual-stage induction into the existing semi-artificial feeding method may further enhance the efficiency of establishing B. ovata infection in ticks, providing a valuable approach for studies of tick-pathogen interactions.

papers.title: Host genomic markers and candidate regions associated with Babesia bovis infection in cattle: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Babesia bovis is one of the most pathogenic agents of bovine babesiosis and remains a major constraint to cattle production in tropical and subtropical regions. This systematic review synthesizes the available evidence on host genomic markers linked to B. bovis in cattle, with emphasis on genome-wide association studies, major histocompatibility complex variants, and host-response studies relevant to marker discovery. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched using a predefined strategy, complemented by targeted searching and citation tracking. The searches identified 1090 records; after removal of 463 duplicates, 627 unique records were screened and 23 reports were retained for structured narrative synthesis. A meta-analysis was not performed because the evidence was heterogeneous in phenotype definition, population, design, and effect measure. Direct host-side genomic evidence remains scarce and is dominated by a small number of population-specific studies. The strongest genome-wide evidence comes from Hereford and Braford cattle, with top SNP signals on BTA1, 2, 5, 6, 12, 16, 17, 18, 24 and 26 and positional candidate genes including ATP8A1, LCP1, LRCH1, QSOX1, FGF2, DSC1, DSC3, FGFR2 and CEBPG. BoLA-DRB3*011:01 was associated with resistance to B. bovis infection in Crioulo Lageano cattle. Overall, host response appears polygenic, weakly heritable, and strongly influenced by immune regulation, breed background, host-vector interaction, and epidemiological context. No single marker is currently validated for routine selection across breeds; future progress will require larger reference populations, improved phenotyping, and independent validation.

papers.title: Tick-borne pathogens in Finnish wildlife: The role of non-native raccoon dog and European hare.
papers.abstract: The role of different host species in the circulation dynamics of tick-borne pathogens (TBPs) in northern ecosystems remains insufficiently characterized, despite the widespread distribution of these pathogens in European wildlife. In particular, the contribution of medium-sized mammals, including non-native species, to TBP circulation is poorly understood. We screened 446 skin samples from nine wildlife species in Finland for multiple zoonotic TBPs to assess pathogen occurrence across host species with particular emphasis on the invasive raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides) and non-native European hare (Lepus europaeus). Borrelia burgdorferi s.l., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and Rickettsia helvetica were the most frequently detected pathogens, with prevalence varying among host species. Babesia spp. was predominantly detected in ungulates, whereas Spiroplasma ixodetis and Borrelia miyamotoi were rare. Raccoon dogs and European hares showed generally low pathogen prevalence, while the highest TBP prevalences were observed in squirrels, hedgehogs, and ungulates. We also screened for two Ixodes-associated endosymbionts (Rickettsiella spp. and Midichloria mitochondrii) as potential indicators of tick exposure. Although Rickettsiella spp. was associated with TBP infections, the low prevalence of both endosymbionts suggests their limited utility as tick bite markers. These findings provide a cross-sectional overview of TBP occurrence in Finnish wildlife and demonstrate that host-pathogen associations vary among species. The relatively low pathogen prevalence observed in the raccoon dog and European hare suggests that these species are unlikely to play a major role in maintaining TBP transmission in northern ecosystems, although they may contribute to tick abundance and dispersal.

papers.title: Identifying counties at elevated acarological risk for reporting high incidence of Lyme disease in the eastern United States.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease, caused primarily by the bite of a nymphal blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) infected with Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto (Bbss), is the most common vector-borne disease in the United States. Counties reporting high Lyme disease incidence (LDI) continue to expand beyond historic foci in the Northeast and Upper Midwest. Identifying areas of expansion aids in targeting efforts to improve Lyme disease awareness in affected communities. Tick surveillance is conducted to track changes in acarological risk for tickborne diseases; the density of host-seeking Bbss-infected I. scapularis nymphs (DIN) is considered the most predictive metric for human LDI. We aimed to identify a threshold in DIN that accurately separated high (≥10 average annual cases/100,000 and ≥3 cases/year; 2022-2023) from low LDI counties in the eastern US. Using previously reported model-derived DIN, we identified 0.98 Bbss-infected nymphs per 1000 m2 as the threshold. Based on this threshold, we classified 18% of eastern counties (487/2695), primarily in the Northeast and Upper Midwest, with both high LDI and elevated acarological risk and 72% (1935/2695) with both low LDI and acarological risk. Another 8% of counties (220/2695), primarily in Michigan, Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio, were predicted to pose elevated acarological risk, but reported low LDI and may reflect areas of emergence that could benefit from expanded tick surveillance and public health outreach. The remaining 2% of counties (53/2695), mainly along the Appalachian Mountains, reported high LDI, but were misclassified as low acarological risk, highlighting the need for additional tick surveillance to improve acarological risk assessments.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: The Lyme disease spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi, maintains a low burden during vertebrate infection. This limitation has historically proven to be particularly challenging for genome-based studies of B. burgdorferi infection and spirochete presence after antibiotic treatment. Here, we used TBDCapSeq, an oligo capture-based next- generation sequencing assay, to demonstrate its utility for genome recovery of B. burgdorferi directly from C3H- and BALB/c-infected mice. Tissue fragments from the ear, heart, tarsus, and infection-site skin were collected at 3 and 6 months post-tick infection from antibiotic-treated and untreated animals. We evaluated 59 tissues from 20 untreated mice and 48 tissues from 17 doxycycline-treated mice for spirochete burden and extent of genome recovery. In the untreated mice, genome recovery from each tissue was determined by the amount of borrelial DNA present in the sequencing library and was highest in the ear and heart, followed by the skin, and lowest in the tarsus. We established that approximately 50% of the genome could be recovered with as few as 10 spirochetes per assay and >90% recovery could be achieved with only 35 spirochete genomes. In the antibiotic-treated mice, trace quantities of fragmented Borrelia DNA were still present in tissues at 3 and 6 months. However, none of the tissue samples from these mice yielded an intact B. burgdorferi genome characteristic of a viable spirochete. Combined, our findings demonstrate that capture sequencing enables genomic analyses of B. burgdorferi directly within animal hosts.IMPORTANCELyme disease, caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, is the most common tick-borne infection in the United States. Low pathogen burden is a major limitation of B. burgdorferi studies in animal hosts and humans that has impacted a wide range of studies ranging from diagnostics, evolutionary analyses, and pathogenesis. It has also contributed to the controversies regarding B. burgdorferi persistence after antibiotic treatment. We show that a next-generation capture sequencing-based approach can readily overcome the current limitations of B. burgdorferi genomic analyses within animal hosts. We successfully recovered abundant genomic information directly from mouse tissues, and we did not find genetic evidence of intact bacteria present after antibiotic treatment. This approach can be employed to gain further insights into B. burgdorferi and provide critical genome data during animal and human infection.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Rodents play a central role as reservoirs of zoonotic pathogens, yet the ecological and meteorological factors affecting pathogen prevalence remain unclear. In this study, a meta-analysis was used to evaluate the influence of host species and meteorological factors on the prevalence of Babesia microti in two common Japanese field mice, Apodemus speciosus and A. argenteus. The data were collected from seven published studies conducted across Japan. To examine the effects of total annual precipitation, average annual temperature, and host species, generalized linear mixed models were employed. The prevalence of the Hobetsu/Otsu-type B. microti was significantly higher in A. speciosus than in A. argenteus, indicating possible differences in reservoir competence and vector preference by Ixodes ovatus, which mainly infests terrestrial rodents. Conversely, the prevalence of the Kobe-type B. microti showed no significant differences between host species; however, it was negatively correlated with increasing precipitation. These findings suggest that meteorological factors may reflect a behavioral mismatch between the tick vectors, Haemaphysalis longicornis and Ixodes nipponensis, and their Apodemus hosts. One possible explanation for these results is that the vectors for Kobe-type B. microti, such as H. longicornis and I. nipponensis, primarily quest on vegetation, and the frequency of host-vector contact decreases when rodents remain in their burrows during heavy rain. This study provides the first quantitative evidence of host-environment interactions impacting rodent-borne babesiosis in Japan. It underscores the importance of considering meteorological and ecological perspectives when forecasting tick-borne disease risks in the context of climate change.

papers.title: Development of bilateral facial nerve palsies while receiving doxycycline for early disseminated Lyme disease.
papers.abstract: Disease progression is uncommon in patients diagnosed with Lyme disease who receive appropriate therapy. Here we report a case of a patient developing bilateral facial nerve palsies while receiving oral doxycycline therapy for early disseminated Lyme disease and review the literature of similar cases. A 58-year-old previously healthy male from the mid-Atlantic area in the U.S. presented with a multifocal erythematous rash consistent with erythema migrans after international travel. His clinical presentation and two-step Lyme-serology testing confirmed a diagnosis of Lyme disease. Four days into initiation of doxycycline therapy, he developed bilateral facial weakness including difficulty raising the corners of his mouth and lifting his eyebrows bilaterally. He experienced neurologic improvement with ongoing antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone and subsequent doxycycline and had complete recovery 7 weeks later. This case describes an uncommon presentation of neuroborreliosis with bilateral facial palsies which developed after initiation of treatment of early disseminated Lyme disease. The manifestations in this case may be due to host immune reaction as seen in other spirochetal diseases. The findings resolved with continued therapy. In our review of the literature, we identified three additional cases of neuroborreliosis which progressed on treatment but also had eventual resolution of signs and symptoms. Clinicians should be aware that facial palsies rarely can occur on therapy for Lyme disease but do not necessarily imply a worse prognosis.

papers.title: Case Report: Atypical cat-scratch disease presenting as referred shoulder pain and deep lymphadenopathy in a pediatric patient.
papers.abstract: Cat-scratch disease (CSD) is a zoonotic infection attributable to Bartonella henselae. Typical clinical manifestations include regional lymphadenopathy accompanied by primary cutaneous lesions that develop following exposure to cats. Although most patients present with typical regional lymphadenopathy, a subset of patients may develop atypical manifestations, which can complicate diagnosis. Owing to the nonspecific clinical features, CSD is prone to misdiagnosis or diagnostic omission. This report describes a pediatric case of atypical cat-scratch disease characterized by initial symptoms of fever and shoulder arthralgia, absence of superficial lymphadenopathy, and involvement of deep lymph nodes. This report aims to broaden clinicians' recognition of the diverse and atypical clinical manifestations of this disease. An 11-year-old female patient presented to the hospital with persistent fever accompanied by left shoulder joint pain and restricted movement of the left upper extremity. Physical examination upon admission revealed no superficial lymphadenopathy or characteristic cutaneous lesions. Following empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, the patient continued to experience recurrent febrile episodes, with persistently elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the shoulder joint and contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the left axillary, supraclavicular, and deep cervical regions. Further history-taking disclosed recent exposure to cats. Histopathological examination of an axillary lymph node biopsy (hematoxylin-eosin staining) revealed suppurative granulomatous lymphadenitis. These H&E histopathological findings are merely supportive rather than confirmatory evidence for CSD, as we failed to perform Bartonella henselae-specific serology, PCR, Warthin-Starry silver staining or immunohistochemistry to identify the pathogen directly. The diagnosis was considered highly suggestive of atypical CSD based on integrated clinical, radiological, epidemiological, and histopathological findings. Upon diagnosis, the patient was administered doxycycline in combination with rifampicin for antimicrobial treatment. The patient's body temperature normalized, shoulder pain progressively resolved, and inflammatory markers returned to reference ranges. During a 3-month follow-up period, no disease recurrence was noted. Shoulder joint mobility was restored to normal, and no significant adverse drug reactions were observed. In pediatric patients presenting with fever of unknown origin accompanied by musculoskeletal symptoms, suboptimal response to conventional anti-infective therapy, and absence of superficial lymphadenopathy, the possibility of atypical cat scratch disease should be considered. A detailed assessment of contact history with domestic animals, along with prompt deep lymph node imaging evaluation and histopathological biopsy, facilitates early and appropriate clinical diagnosis. Implementation of targeted antimicrobial therapy may improve clinical outcomes in affected children.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Dasatinib is a second-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) used in Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and chylothorax is one of its rare but serious lymphatic complications. We encountered a 14-year-old boy with Ph + acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) who developed bilateral chylothorax while on dasatinib, with concurrent B. henselae infection (cat-scratch disease) confirmed in the pleural fluid. Prompted by this index case, we performed a systematic review of the literature to explore the potential association between dasatinib-associated chylothorax and Bartonella henselae infection. We searched multiple databases up to March 2026 and identified 24 cases of TKI-associated chylothorax and 11 cases of leukemia-related cat-scratch disease. In our index case, the pleural fluid triglyceride concentration reached 20.40 mmol/L (≈1806 mg/dL)-the highest value reported to date-and mNGS detected B. henselae together with other organisms. After dasatinib was discontinued and the patient received chest drainage, somatostatin, fasting, and anti-infective therapy with doxycycline plus rifampicin, imaging showed near-complete resolution of the effusion, and repeat mNGS confirmed clearance of B. henselae. A formal causality assessment using the Naranjo scale gave a score of 7, indicating a "probable" adverse drug reaction. This case illustrates that lymphatic and infectious complications can coincide in the same patient. Dasatinib-mediated inhibition of Src family kinases may simultaneously impair lymphatic endothelial integrity and suppress T-cell-mediated immune surveillance, thereby facilitating both chylous leakage and opportunistic infection. Clinicians managing paediatric patients receiving long-term dasatinib therapy should remain vigilant for both lymphatic complications and atypical opportunistic infections.

papers.title: Giving a Rat's: Acquisition of Baseline Health Data on Native Australian Rodents During a Conservation Translocation.
papers.abstract: Little is known about the baseline health status of Australia's native rodents. The resultant knowledge gaps are problematic for wildlife translocations, as assessing disease risk is integral to translocation planning and outcomes. A disease risk analysis was conducted for the conservation translocation of native rodents to Dirk Hartog Island, Western Australia. This analysis resulted in a recommendation for a multidisciplinary project to reduce knowledge gaps about the health status of Shark Bay mice (Pseudomys gouldii) and greater-stick-nest rats (Leporillus conditor). Between 2021 and 2022, 130 Shark Bay mice and 122 greater stick-nest rats were translocated to Dirk Hartog Island. Mucosal swabs, whole blood, faeces, and ectoparasites were collected from a subset of these individuals. Molecular testing for four infectious agents was performed, parasite burdens and haematological parameters were examined, and relationships between these variables, health metrics and post-translocation short-term survival were assessed. Necropsies with routine histological assessment on translocation mortalities were performed where feasible. Several indicators of non-infectious factors contributing to morbidity or mortality were found, highlighting the need to iteratively evaluate translocation strategies. There was also an apparent absence of some host-specific parasites, suggesting that active approaches to parasite conservation during translocations should be considered. Molecular evidence of herpesviruses, a paramyxovirus, Bartonella sp., Trypanosoma sp. and Mycoplasma spp. were detected among the translocated animals. Although not associated with morbidity or short-term mortality in this study, the disease potential of these agents is still present. Overall, these results contribute important new data on health baselines for both species, which will assist in informing future conservation planning.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Vector-borne diseases (VBDs) represent a concern for animal and public health, and wildlife surveillance is valuable for their monitoring. The occurrence, molecular diversity and host distribution of tick-borne protozoa (TBP: Babesia spp., Theileria spp. and Hepatozoon spp.) and Bartonella spp. were investigated in wild carnivores from three regions of northwestern Italy. Spleen samples from 690 wild carnivores were screened for TBP and/or Bartonella spp. by PCR followed by sequencing. Among the 503 carnivores screened for TBP, 197 animals (39.2%) tested positive for at least one targeted protozoan species, including 87 positives for Babesia spp. (17.3%) and 120 for Hepatozoon spp. (23.9%). Bartonella spp. DNA was additionally detected in only one of the 363 animals tested (0.3%). Sequencing identified Babesia sp. badger types A and C in badgers, B. vulpes in foxes and B. canis in wolves, Hepatozoon canis in wolves and foxes, H. martis in stone martens and Hepatozoon sp. in stone and pine martens. Phylogenetic analyses supported the host-associated clustering of the detected lineages, confirming the molecular identification. These findings indicate the frequent occurrence of different TBP in wild carnivores from northwestern Italy, with marked host associated patterns, contributing to our understanding of VBD epidemiology with a One Health approach.

papers.title: Cat scratch disease with fever and lymphadenopathy without definite cat exposure diagnosed via tissue metagenomic next-generation sequencing technology: a case report.
papers.abstract: Cat scratch disease (CSD), a disease caused by Bartonella henselae (B. henselae), is often associated with exposure to cats. However, in rare cases, a history of cat exposure is absent, and thus achieving a definitive diagnosis may be challenging. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) is a relatively new technology that can analyze pathogens without introducing inherent biases. In this report, we describe a case of CSD diagnosed via mNGS, which supports the use of mNGS in identifying rare types of pathogenic infection. A 54-year-old male exhibited fever and headache of unknown cause, with a history of working at a chicken farm and no clear cat exposure. Routine antibiotic treatment for infection was ineffective. Lymph node biopsy demonstrated granulomas accompanied by chronic suppurative inflammation and abscess formation. A biopsy sample from the parotid lymph node was subjected to mNGS, which revealed the presence of B. henselae and led to a subsequent diagnosis of CSD. After treatment with azithromycin, the patient recovered and was discharged. At the 3-month telephone follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic. CSD in patients with prolonged fever plus culture-negative granulomatous lymphadenopathy or similar compatible findings, even when the exposure history is atypical，and mNGS, as an effective examination method, can aid in arriving at a definitive diagnosis.
